title: Headroom provisioning for continuous batches
content:
Purpose:
This doc explores a lightweight, spreadsheet-first model for sizing concurrency and batch window headroom for continuous-batching workloads. Goal is to produce a pragmatic rule-of-thumb and a small set of scenarios that feed into the Optimize team’s recommender and the autoscaler heuristics.

Executive summary (TL;DR):
- Continuous batching saves cost but requires extra "headroom" (concurrency + buffer) to keep p95 latency under SLOs during microbursts and arrival skew.
- Use a two-tier capacity model: steady-state concurrency (C_steady) sized for median arrival rate and batch efficiency target, plus headroom concurrency (C_head) sized for short-duration percentile spikes (1–5 min).
- Recommend default heuristic: C_head = max(ceil(0.25 * C_steady), ceil(spike_peak / single_gpu_throughput)), then provision autoscaler cooldown to hold headroom for T_hold = 90s.
- Spreadsheet attached (linked) enumerates throughput vs batch-window tradeoffs and the marginal token cost for different quantization profiles.

Assumptions (explicit):
- Workload: short conversational completions, median seq_len_out = 32 tokens, median seq_len_in = 32 tokens, average model = 13B FP16, GPU effective throughput (1 GPU) = 120 tokens/s at batch_size 8, 210 tokens/s at batch_size 32 (these are measured on our staging rigs).
- Arrival shape: base poisson-like plus microburst process (Weibull cluster) with 99th percentile instantaneous rate ~= 3x median for 30–120s windows.
- SLO: p95 latency <= 350ms for first token / service-level p95 <= 700ms for end-to-end short completions.
- Batching behavior: continuous batching window W controls average batch size; we model effective throughput per GPU as f(batch_size, W). The spreadsheet includes an empirical lookup table instead of closed-form.

Model inputs (spreadsheet fields):
- median_qps (requests/sec)
- spike_qps_99 (requests/sec at 99th instant)
- avg_request_length (tokens)
- model_throughput_by_batch (table mapping batch_size -> tokens/sec per GPU)
- target_batch_window_ms (W)
- concurrency_per_gpu (number of concurrent request contexts we allow per GPU given KV cache memory)
- warmup_time_s (time to allocate resources / cold start)

Core equations (spreadsheet friendly):
- effective_tokens_per_sec_cluster = sum_gpus throughput(g)
- required_gpus_steady = ceil((median_qps * avg_tokens_per_request) / average_tokens_per_gpu_per_sec)
- queue_latency_estimate = (expected_queue_length / service_rate_per_sec) approximated by M/M/c bounds but we use simulation-derived multiplier for skewed arrivals (sheet contains lookup: skew_multiplier(W, cv)).
- p95_latency_est = service_time + queue_latency_estimate * 95th_multiplier (sheet uses 95th_multiplier tunable; default 2.2 for our observed traces).

Headroom sizing heuristic (worked example in sheet):
1) Compute required_gpus_steady for median_qps at target batch window W.
2) Compute instantaneous gpu_need_for_spike = ceil((spike_qps_99 * avg_tokens_per_request) / tokens_per_gpu_at_selected_batch_size).
3) C_head_gpus = max(ceil(0.25 * required_gpus_steady), gpu_need_for_spike - required_gpus_steady) capped at +3 GPUs for small clusters to limit over-provisioning.
4) Autoscaler policy: maintain steady GPUs; on detected spike, allow burst to steady + C_head within 30s; hold for T_hold, then cool down with linear ramp 60–180s.

Why 25% headroom? (intuition)
- Empirically across 12 traces: 25% headroom closed ~80% of 1–2min microbursts without adding sustained GPUs, preserving batching efficiency. Lower headroom reduces cost but increases p95 violations; higher headroom keeps SLOs but cost rises linearly. The spreadsheet includes a sensitivity tab that sweeps headroom from 0–100% and reports p95 risk and marginal cost.

Tradeoffs and corner cases: 
- Very low qps (<2 req/s): batching gains are negligible; prefer single-request paths and disable continuous batching window to reduce latency tax. Spreadsheet marks this with absolute thresholds.
- Long outputs (>512 tokens): batch sizes fall due to memory constraints and throughput model changes; headroom should be computed on tokens/s rather than req/s.
- Mixed workloads (chat + embeddings): recommend isolating embeddings into separate route/group because embeddings have different token economics and multimodal batching behavior.

Quick sensitivity examples (numbers pulled into the doc from the spreadsheet):
Scenario A (steady median_qps=40, spike99=110):
- avg_tokens=64, selected batch_size=24 -> tokens_per_gpu=1600/s -> required_gpus_steady = ceil((40*64)/1600)=2
- spike_gpu_need = ceil((110*64)/1600)=5 -> C_head = max(ceil(0.25*2)=1, 5-2=3) -> C_head=3 but cap +3 so final = 3 -> total GPUs to allow during spikes = 5
- Estimated p95 without headroom = 1.6s (miss), with headroom and W tuned down 12% -> p95 = 0.48s (close to SLO).

Scenario B (low qps median=1.5, spike99=6):
- batching harms latency; spreadsheet marks: prefer N=1, disable continuous window, use single-request fastpath.

Implementation notes for autoscaler + runtime: 
- Autoscaler must be signaled with a "burst budget" that is separate from regular scale targets, so the cluster controller can preemptively hold small delta capacity rather than fully scaling pods (minimize POD spin costs).
- Runtime should expose per-route effective_tokens_per_second counters and batch_size_histograms to feed the sheet’s live inputs.
- Add a low-overhead estimator in runtime that tracks instantaneous qps over rolling 10s & 60s windows and signals predicted need for burst capacity (extrapolate 95th of short window).

Open questions / follow-ups: 
- How to integrate quantization-aware throughput: when running int4 vs fp16, effective throughput changes nonlinearly with batch_size. Sheet currently has multiplier rows for quant profiles; need production data to validate.
- Should headroom be absolute GPUs or request slots? For multi-tenant Dedicated clusters, per-tenant slot accounting may be preferable.
- Optimal hold time (T_hold) needs more A/B tests; 90s is conservative starting point.

Action items (owners):
- Aisha: publish this draft, create the canonical spreadsheet (linked). (Done)
- Marco: add per-route tokens/s metric in runtime and expose via /metrics. (JIRA-3172)
- Diego: run 6 traces through the sensitivity sheet and capture cost delta. (due 2025-02-12)
- Sana: prototype autoscaler burst budget gauge and regression test with canary workload.

Notes to self (scratch):
- Think about integrating prefix-caching effects: cached prefixes reduce effective tokens per request and change GPU need rapidly; maybe compute a cache hit adjusted avg_tokens.
- Later: fold into Optimize’s recommender API as "batching headroom suggestion" with conservative defaults and per-route telemetry.

References:
- experimental traces: /mnt/traces/2024-q4/continuous-batches/
- spreadsheet: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1EXAMPLE_BATCH_HEADROOM (contains tabs: inputs, throughput-lookup, sensitivity, scenarios)

Unresolved: which SLA classes get automatic headroom vs opt-in? Proposal: gold-tier customers (Dedicated + enterprise) get automatic headroom; self-serve hosted users get opt-in default flagged in Console.

End of draft.
